name: Daniel J. Crothers
description: Concurred with majority opinion, delivering the opinion of the court.

name: Daniel J. Crothers
description: Concurred, argued that the abortion law is unconstitutionally vague, particularly its health-risk exception, and cannot be severed, thus invalidating it entirely.

name: Jon J. Jensen, C.J.
description: Dissented, argued that the district court erred in finding the abortion law unconstitutionally vague and that Article I, Section 1 does not protect a broad right to abortion conflicting with the law.

name: Jerod E. Tufte
description: Dissented, argued that the majority incorrectly applied a stricter vagueness standard to natural rights and allowed a pre-enforcement facial challenge based on hypothetical future conduct.

name: Douglas A. Bahr
description: Concurred, argued that H.B. 1340 is a valid exercise of the legislature's constitutional authority to create political subdivisions and define the powers of home rule cities, and that it preempts Fargo's ordinances.

name: Crothers, Justice
description: Concurred, argued that S.B. 2015 violated the single subject rule of the North Dakota Constitution, rendering the entire bill void.

name: Jensen, Chief Justice
description: Concurred, argued that while the legislation violated the single subject rule, the underlying action would have been permissible, and the judgment should be stayed for 30 days to allow the legislature to re-enact the legislation constitutionally.

name: McEvers, Justice
description: Concurred, agreed that the legislation violated the single subject rule and that the judgment should be stayed for 30 days, but did not speculate on the likelihood of the legislation surviving further consideration.

name: Gary H. Lee, D.J.
description: Concurred with Justice McEvers' special concurrence.

name: TUFTE, JUSTICE
description: Concurred, arguing that Kollie failed to demonstrate his public trial rights were violated by unrecorded sidebars, that jury instructions on murder were not erroneous, that double jeopardy was not violated by convictions for murder and aggravated assault, and that while admitting the victim's video was error, it was harmless.

name: MCEVERS, JUSTICE
description: Concurred, argued that the appeal is moot because Isaak died, no substitution was sought, no restitution was ordered, and no collateral consequences exist, and that abatement ab initio is inconsistent with victims' constitutional rights.

name: Jon J. Jensen, C.J.
description: Concurred, argued that the North Dakota Constitution guarantees a fundamental right to abortion to preserve a woman's life or health, and the challenged statute is not narrowly tailored to achieve compelling state interests.

name: Tufte, Justice
description: Concurred, argued that the 'life or health' exception for abortion should be understood as a right of self-defense, making the statute unconstitutional for not providing an exception for life-saving abortions.

name: Lisa Fair McEvers
description: Concurred specially, argued that North Dakota's constitutional rights may be broader than those under the U.S. Constitution, supporting the injunction on narrow grounds.

name: Daniel J. Crothers
description: Concurred, argued with Justice McEvers' special concurrence.

name: Daniel D. Narum, D.J.
description: Concurred, argued with Justice McEvers' special concurrence.

name: Jerod E. Tufte
description: Concurred, argued that the Secretary of State misapplied the law by invalidating all signatures notarized by a single notary based on an inference of fraud from some inconsistent signatures, and that each notarial act must be challenged separately.

name: Jon J. Jensen
description: Concurred, argued that quick-take procedures were available for the sewer project and the district court did not abuse its discretion in excluding evidence based on an incorrect interpretation of zoning ordinances.

name: Gerald W. VandeWalle
description: Concurred, arguing that the North Dakota Constitution preserves the right to a jury trial for municipal ordinance violations that carried potential penalties of imprisonment or significant fines at the time of its adoption, and this right applies to the current infraction.
